title: Access Control, Intrusion and Building Automation: One Design, Not Three Systems
description:
At the ASIS Québec 2026 Symposium last week, Auckland-based ICT framed the conversation around one question: how can access control, intrusion detection and building automation work as one platform instead of three? It is the same question we ask at the start of every design engagement in Wellington and Auckland.

Many New Zealand sites end up with three systems bought at three different times. Each has its own head-end, its own user database and its own maintenance contract. The result is duplicated credentials, alarms that are not linked to door events, and former staff who are removed from one system but stay active in another. Our design process starts with how the site actually operates: who moves where, at what hours, and what should happen when an event fires. From there we specify the controllers, integrations and cabling. A forced-door alarm, a schedule change and an after-hours building rule then all sit in one logic model. Getting that architecture right on paper costs far less than untangling it after handover.

If you are planning a fit-out, an upgrade or a consolidation of legacy systems, send us a message to book a design review.

title: Deepfake Callers and Fake Job Applicants Are Now a Physical Security Problem
description:
ASIS International's latest Security Management Highlight episode features Tom Cross, head of threat research at GetReal Security. He explains how AI-enabled deepfakes now produce recorded and live audio and video that are convincing enough to get fake job applicants hired and to let fake authorities walk away with confidential information.

For New Zealand businesses, the physical security consequence is direct. An access card is only as trustworthy as the process that issued it. Suppose a convincing video call passes an interview, or a voice call from a supposed manager authorises a contractor credential. The door hardware will then do exactly what it is told. Wellington and Auckland organisations with lean reception and facilities teams are especially exposed, because credential requests are often approved by phone or email under time pressure. The controls are not exotic. Verify any new credential or visitor escalation through a second channel. Check identity in person before a card is issued. Make contractor access time-limited by default. Run audit reports that flag credentials nobody has sponsored.

Review how your organisation approves a new access card this week. If the answer is a single email, send us a message and we can help tighten the process.

title: Your Building Management System Is on the Network. Who Is Securing It?
description:
Johnson Controls released a white paper last week on AI-augmented attacks against operational technology. It cites the thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities found by Anthropic this year and makes the case for a zero-trust overlay on OT systems.

Our view is that this lands hardest on the systems New Zealand organisations think about least. In many Wellington and Auckland buildings, access controllers, CCTV recorders, intercoms and building management systems share networks with corporate IT. Yet they are often installed by one contractor, patched by nobody, and owned by whichever team signed the original invoice. AI is shortening the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited. That makes firmware untouched since commissioning a live risk, not a technical footnote. As an integrator, we treat security devices as network assets. They are segmented, inventoried and patched on a schedule, and they are handed over with documented credentials rather than defaults. That discipline matters more than any single product choice.

If you are unsure which security devices are on your network or when they were last updated, reach out and we can help you build that inventory.

title: What Happens After an Incident When Your Installer Cannot Prove Compliance
description:
After a break-in or a failed door, the first questions from an insurer, assessor or board are rarely about camera resolution. They are about who installed the system, whether that person was licensed, and whether the maintenance records hold up.

The brief we often receive from New Zealand clients is to take over an existing system from a previous provider. Our approach starts with the paperwork before the hardware. We check that work is carried out by staff holding the certificates of approval required under the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act. We confirm that access-controlled doors on a compliance schedule are recorded correctly. We also make sure every service visit leaves a documented trail. At handover, the client receives as-built drawings, device lists and maintenance history in a form they can produce on request. The outcome is not just a working system. It is a Wellington or Auckland business that can show, quickly and in writing, that its security was installed and maintained properly by accountable people. That evidence is what reduces risk exposure when something goes wrong.

If you are not confident your current records would stand up after an incident, send us a message to book a compliance review.

title: Poll: Who Owns the Security of Your Building's Connected Systems?
description:
ASIS International closed out Cybersecurity Awareness Month with a simple observation. Cybersecurity now touches every security discipline, and threats once confined to a single domain have far-reaching consequences. That raises a practical question for every New Zealand organisation.

Who owns the security of your access control, CCTV, intercom and building management systems? In many Wellington and Auckland buildings, IT manages the network, facilities manages the building, and security manages the doors. The connected devices that sit across all three often end up owned by nobody. That gap is where unpatched recorders, default passwords and forgotten contractor accounts live. Our position is clear. Every connected security device needs one named owner, backed by joint governance between IT, facilities and security. Shared responsibility without a single accountable person usually means no responsibility at all.

title: Who Has the Keys? Tying Key Management to Your Access Credentials
description:
ICT shared a case study this week from the City of Mooresville, where shared vehicle keys kept going missing with no record of who took them or when. The fix wasn't more padlocks. It was key management tied to the badge staff already carry.

The same problem is common in New Zealand. Fleet keys at council depots, plant room keys in Wellington office towers and master keys at Auckland logistics yards often still sit on a hook board or in a manual key safe with a paper sign-out sheet. When ASIS New Zealand designs access control, we treat physical keys as credentials, just like doors. Linking an electronic key cabinet to the access control platform gives you one card, one audit trail and one permissions model across doors and keys. When you revoke a staff member's access, their key rights go with it. Every checkout is logged against a named person, and the help desk can confirm a key is available before sending anyone across site.

If your keys still live on a hook board, send us a message to book an access control review. We'll map where your keys go and what it would take to bring them into your existing system.

title: Bank, Logistics Yard, Data Centre: One Access Platform, Three Different Jobs
description:
ICT made a point this week that applies well beyond its stand at The Security Event Asia: every site asks something different of an access control system. A bank branch needs silent duress alarms and a vault that only opens for two authorised people. A logistics site needs to know who is still on site when the fire alarm sounds. A data centre needs to stop tailgating before anyone reaches the data hall.

For New Zealand businesses, the takeaway isn't about one product. When access control, intrusion detection and building automation run as separate silos, they leave gaps. The alarm panel doesn't know who badged in, the muster list is a guess, and every subsystem needs its own training. Integrated platforms close those gaps and let technicians learn one system across very different sites. For multi-site operators spread across Auckland, Wellington and the regions, that consistency matters as much as the feature list. The real design question is how far to integrate. Tighter integration adds value, but it also concentrates risk. Network segmentation and failover planning belong in the brief from day one.

If you're running separate systems that don't talk to each other, reach out. We'll walk through what integration would look like across your sites.

title: Five Physical Security Myths We Still Hear From New Zealand Businesses
description:
Most security gaps we find on New Zealand sites don't come from missing equipment. They come from assumptions nobody has tested.

Here are five we hear regularly. First, more cameras mean better security. Without clear coverage goals, sensible retention settings and someone reviewing footage, cameras only record what already happened. Second, a locked door is a secure door. That stops being true once the closer wears out, the strike drifts out of alignment or staff prop the door open on a warm afternoon. Third, monitored means someone will turn up. Monitoring and response are different services, and many businesses don't know which one they're paying for. Fourth, we're too small to be a target. Opportunistic offenders look for easy access, not company size. Fifth, once it's installed, it's done. Systems drift as staff change, firmware ages and fit-outs move walls. ASIS New Zealand starts every review by testing what's actually on site rather than trusting what's on the drawing.

title: Leaving School or Uni This Summer? Security Technology Is a Real Trade
description:

A field technician might commission an access control system in a Wellington office in the morning and diagnose a camera network fault at an Auckland warehouse in the afternoon. The industry needs people who can wire a door correctly and who also understand IP addressing, cybersecurity basics and how a building is actually used. At ASIS New Zealand, people starting out learn alongside experienced engineers on live projects, building hands-on skills with the platforms our clients rely on. title: ISO 45001 on a Security Install: What It Changes for You
description:
November and December are peak months for security work in New Zealand. Fit-outs race to finish before the Christmas shutdown, and contractors across Auckland and Wellington share ceiling space, risers and scissor lifts. That's exactly when site safety gets squeezed.

ISO 45001 is the international standard for occupational health and safety management. For a client, the certificate on the wall matters less than what sits behind it. That means documented risk assessments for work at height and in ceiling voids, clear permit-to-work processes, proper contractor inductions, and incident reporting that leads to fixes rather than blame. Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, a business that brings contractors onto site shares duties for their safety. The safety system your security contractor runs therefore affects your own risk directly. At ASIS New Zealand, health and safety planning starts at the quoting stage, well before anyone climbs a ladder. Ask a prospective contractor how they manage safety on site. The answer tells you a lot about how they'll manage the rest of the job.

If you're planning security work before the summer shutdown, send us a message. We'll talk through how we'd run it safely on your site.

title: No Manager On Site: Can Unstaffed Access Really Be Secure?
description:
"It means we now don't have to have a manager onsite." That's Terry King, Managing Director of Safeguard, in an ICT case study this week on a Protege GX system installed by Millennium Technology. At Safeguard, a new customer has their PIN seconds after registering and paying.

Unstaffed and self-service sites are spreading across New Zealand, from storage facilities and 24/7 gyms to co-working spaces and after-hours depots. The commercial case is obvious. The security case is where the debate lives. Taking the person off site removes both a deterrent and an eyewitness, so the system has to carry more of the load. That means credential issuance tied to verified identity, instant revocation, camera coverage at every entry point, and monitoring that someone actually acts on. ASIS New Zealand's view is that an unstaffed site can be as secure as a staffed one, and sometimes more secure. That only holds when access, video and monitoring are designed together and audited regularly. Automation without oversight just moves the risk somewhere nobody is looking.

Where do you land? Would you trust a fully unstaffed site with your business or your belongings, and what would it take to convince you? Drop a comment below.
